text: Put-call parity tells you how a call and put relate to each other, but not what either is worth on its own. The binomial model is the first framework in this course that actually prices an option from scratch — by chopping time into small steps, letting the stock only go up or down at each step, and working backward from expiration using no-arbitrage logic the whole way.

At each step the stock moves up by a factor u or down by a factor d, building out a tree of possible paths. The trick that makes this an arbitrage-free pricing tool is the risk-neutral probability, p. It's not a forecast of what will actually happen — it's defined so that, under p, the stock's expected return exactly equals the risk-free rate. That lets you discount expected payoffs at the risk-free rate and get a clean, arbitrage-free price without ever needing real-world probabilities or risk preferences.

Pricing works backward. First, at the final layer of the tree, compute the payoff directly at every possible ending stock price. Then, at every earlier node, the option's value is the discounted, risk-neutral expected value of its two possible successors. Repeat that one layer at a time until you land back at today. Because each step only looks one node ahead, this same machinery prices American options almost for free — at each node you just compare the value of holding against the value of exercising immediately and take the larger one.

Here's a two-step example. Stock at 100, strike 100, up factor 1.1, down factor 0.9, five percent risk-free rate. The risk-neutral probability works out to about 0.756. The final stock prices are 121, 99, and 81, giving payoffs of 21, 0, and 0. Stepping back through the tree, the up node is worth about 15.11, the down node is worth zero, and the option's price today comes out to about 10.87 — entirely from no-arbitrage logic.

As you add more steps, the binomial tree's price converges to Black-Scholes — it's the same no-arbitrage logic in discrete time. Up next, lesson fourteen: the Black-Scholes model, the continuous-time, closed-form version of this same idea.
